Fraud Compliance Identity Management Kyc Product Management An Identity & Fraud PM’s Love Letter to KBA: Some Legacies Are Worth Killing Shreya Shashank 6 min read · Oct 31, 2026 -- Listen Share Why I replaced knowledge-based authentication with layered identity verification, and what happened to conversion and compliance Dear KBA, we had a good run. You were there when the internet needed something, anything, to check who was on the other side of the screen. You were cheap, you were familiar, and you came bundled in a vendor contract nobody reread. But it’s time I told you the truth. You stopped working a long time ago. It’s not me. It’s you. If your onboarding still asks people which car they financed in 2014, I have bad news. Mostly fraudsters and wondow shoppers are passing that quiz. Your real customers are failing it. As a Identity and risk PM, I spent the better part of a year ripping knowledge-based authentication (KBA) out of every flow and replacing it with layered identity verification. Meaningful revenue that had been quietly passing through KBA for years, started quietly moving through the new IDV flows. And ooof what a delictae dance between conversion, fraud and conversion quality! Here’s what I learned, including the parts nobody tells you. KBA is broken, and it has been for years KBA, or “out-of-wallet” questions, works by pulling facts from credit bureau and public records and asking the user to confirm them. Old addresses, loan amounts, phone numbers. The theory: only the real person knows. Press enter or click to view image in full size The theory died somewhere between the large bureau breaches of the last decade and the rise of cheap data brokers. Today, the people most likely to know your user’s old addresses are the ones who bought them. NIST’s digital identity guidelines have discouraged KBA for identity proofing since 2017. Some of the industry just kept using it because it was there, it was cheap, and the vendor contract auto-renewed. Meanwhile, look at who fails KBA: Thin-file users : young adults, recent immigrants, people who’ve mostly rented. No credit history, no questions, or worse, questions about someone else. People with messy histories : a dozen addresses, a divorce, a name change. Real life is not a multiple-choice quiz. Older users : who honestly do not remember which lender held their auto loan eleven years ago. Neither do I. So you end up with a check that’s weak against professional fraud and strong against your actual customers. That’s not a security control. That’s a conversion tax with a compliance sticker on it. Why growth teams love KBA (and why that’s the trap) In regulated industries like fintech and insurance, you can’t skip identity verification. You need guardrails that keep you compliant. KBA became the comfortable middle ground: compliance gets its checkbox, and growth teams love it because most people pass. A quiz about your old addresses feels a lot less scary than “now scan your driver’s license.” And that’s exactly the slippery slope. KBA’s high pass rate looks like great conversion. It isn’t. KBA lets most people in, including the ones you really don’t want: Fraudsters pass easily. They bought the answers. A quiz built on breached data is an open-book exam for them. Low-quality customers sail through too. Low-intent users, people who’ll churn, lapse or never pay. They count as conversions on day one and as losses three months later. Meanwhile, some of your best customers still fail. The thin-file, the recently moved, the honestly forgetful. So you get the worst of both worlds: the wrong people in, some of the right people out, and a dashboard telling you everything is fine. The fix isn’t to swing the other way and make everyone scan a passport. It’s to stop celebrating top-of-funnel pass rates and start measuring conversion quality : how many verified users are real, stay, and pay. Once we put downstream fraud, early lapses and chargebacks next to the pass rate, the case for replacing KBA made itself. Compliant guardrails, less friction for good users, more friction for risky ones. That’s the trade you actually want. The real problem: one path, no exits Here’s the part that took me longest to see. The issue wasn’t just KBA. It was that KBA was the only path. You maybe be a criminal or YTom Cruise- no matter what teh risk profile was- you’d just get KBA. Pass or fail it on your time. Any time a user-facing flow has a single point of failure, you’re not designing for verification. You’re designing for drop-off. What I built instead- Layered verification The replacement wasn’t “swap KBA for selfie.” It was a set of options that escalate based on risk and give people somewhere to go when one method doesn’t work for them: Start passive. Phone ownership , phone possession and carrier signals, device signals, and data matching (name, date of birth, SSN against authoritative sources). For a large share of users, this is enough, and they never see a hard verification step at all. Escalate only when needed. If passive checks are inconclusive or risk signals fire, step up to document + selfie, rather than forcing everyone through the heaviest check. Always offer an alternate route.
